body.text: What makes Astrobiology one of the most revealing subjects in empirical research? Primary observations and reproducible data continue to reshape how scientists model the physical world.

Astrobiology is an interdisciplinary field of scientific study that aims to answer fundamental questions about the origin, distribution and evolution of life in the universe. Its scope includes the origin and evolution of life on Earth, the search for extraterrestrial life, and the future prospects for life in the universe.
Astrobiology is founded on the premise that life may exist beyond Earth, and posits that studying how life arose and developed on Earth may inform our search for life elsewhere.

Astrobiology is closely related to (but distinct from) exobiology: by definition, exobiology is focused on the study of life beyond Earth, including human spaceflight and the prospects for human exploration of other planets.

body.text: Research in astrobiology builds on interdisciplinary collaborations between experts in disciplines such as astronomy, astrochemistry, the Earth sciences, and the life and environmental sciences.

The scope of the research includes the exploration of potentially habitable environments in our Solar System, the discovery and characterization of potentially habitable exoplanets, elucidating conditions on the early Earth that may have given rise to life, the origin and evolution of terrestrial life, and the identification of biosignatures that may enable us to detect life elsewhere.
Origin and growth

Astrobiology has its origins in the mid-20th century. The term was first proposed by the Russian astronomer Gavriil Tikhov in 1953. It is etymologically derived from the Greek ἄστρον, "star", βίος, "life", and -λογία, -logia, "study".

A close synonym is exobiology from the Greek Έξω, "external", βίος, "life", and -λογία, -logia, "study", coined by American molecular biologist Joshua Lederberg, exobiology is considered to have a narrow scope limited to the search for and study of life external to Earth.

Another associated term is xenobiology, from the Greek ξένος, "foreign", βίος, "life", and -λογία, "study", coined by American science fiction writer Robert Heinlein in his 1954 work The Star Beast, xenobiology is now used in a more specialised sense, referring to 'biology based on foreign chemistry', whether of extraterrestrial or terrestrial (typically synthetic) origin.

From the beginning, research in astrobiology focused on the search for extraterrestrial life and the potential for life to exist on other planets. Important factors that underpinned research were the advent of space exploration, and technological developments in observational astronomy that ultimately led to the discovery and characterization of exoplanets.

An important early example is NASA's Viking program (1976), the first to successfully land spacecraft on Mars and search in situ for evidence of life. This mission laid the foundation for the development of astrobiology as a major objective within the purview of the space program.

A parallel development was the advent of the SETI program, enabled by technological developments in communications and radio astronomy that provide the potential to detect signals from extraterrestrial intelligence.

In 1971, NASA's Project Cyclops, developed a framework designed to optimize searches of radio frequencies in the electromagnetic spectrum for signals transmitted by extraterrestrial life outside of the Solar System.

While the potential for extraterrestrial life, especially intelligent life, has been a topic of philosophical discussion throughout human history, the advance in technology has rendered the question potentially verifiable, and thus a valid line of scientific inquiry, planetary scientist David Grinspoon had described it as a field of natural philosophy, grounding speculation on the unknown in known scientific theory.

Astrobiology has developed into an inherently interdisciplinary endeavor that presents both challenges and opportunities for those engaged in it. The field began to expand and diversify in the 1980s and 1990s as new discoveries and technologies emerged, most notably the discovery of exoplanets.
Meanwhile, the discovery of microbial life in extreme environments on Earth, such as deep-sea hydrothermal vents, helped to clarify the feasibility of potential life existing in harsh conditions.
The advent of new techniques for the detection of biosignatures, such as the use of stable isotopes, also played a significant role in the evolution of the field.

Integral within the scope of modern astrobiology are the search for biosignatures, both within and beyond our Solar System, the exploration of limits to habitability, and the fundamental question of life's origins, both on Earth and potentially elsewhere. All of these investigations are underpinned by interdisciplinary research.

Exoplanets are discovered and their orbits characterized by traditional methods of observational astronomy (photometry, spectroscopy, the Doppler effect), enabling those in circumstellar habitable zones to be identified, and their masses estimated.

However, the next step, to search for life on those planets, requires expertise in chemistry, biology and the geosciences to determine what observations could provide a convincing detection. If a secure detection is made, expertise beyond these traditional science disciplines will be needed to fully understand the philosophical, cultural and sociological implications of our discovery.

To better understanding the limits of planetary habitability, astrobiologists investigate potential environments beyond Earth that could support life, such as Mars, Europa and other icy moons within our Solar System, as well as exoplanets. This research is informed by research into terrestrial extremophiles that populate austere regions of Earth, such as volcanic and deep-sea environments.

Research within this topic is conducted utilizing the methodology of the geosciences, especially geobiology, for astrobiological applications. The search for biosignatures involves the identification of signs of past or present life in the form of organic compounds, isotopic abundances characteristic of biological processes, and microbial fossils.

Research within this topic is conducted utilizing the methodology of planetary and environmental science, especially atmospheric science, for astrobiological applications, and may be conducted through remote sensing or in situ missions.
Astrobiology also concerns the study of the origin and early evolution of life on Earth, with the goal of understanding the conditions that are necessary for life to form on other planets.

This research seeks to understand how life emerged from non-living matter and how it evolved to become the diverse array of organisms we see today. Research within this topic is conducted utilising the methodology of paleosciences, especially paleobiology, for astrobiological applications.
Theoretical foundations
Planetary habitability
Astrobiological research makes a number of simplifying assumptions when studying the necessary components for planetary habitability.

Carbon is the fourth most abundant element in the universe, and the energy required to make or break a bond is at just the appropriate level for building stable, reactive molecules. The fact that carbon atoms bond readily to other carbon atoms allows for the building of extremely long and complex molecules.
As such, astrobiological research presumes that the vast majority of life forms in the Milky Way galaxy are based on carbon chemistries, as are all life forms on Earth.

However, theoretical astrobiology entertains the potential for other organic molecular bases for life, thus astrobiological research often focuses on identifying environments that have the potential to support life based on the presence of organic compounds.

Liquid water provides an excellent environment for the formation of complicated carbon-based molecules, and is generally considered necessary for life as we know it to exist. Thus, astrobiological research presumes that extraterrestrial life similarly depends upon access to liquid water, and often focuses on identifying environments that have the potential to support liquid water.
Some researchers posit environments of water-ammonia mixtures as possible solvents for hypothetical types of biochemistry.

Where organisms adaptively evolve to the conditions of the environments in which they reside, environmental stability is considered necessary for life to exist. This presupposes the necessity of stable temperature, pressure, and radiation levels, resultantly, astrobiological research focuses on planets orbiting Sun-like red dwarf stars.

This is because very large stars have relatively short lifetimes, meaning that life might not have time to emerge on planets orbiting them, very small stars provide so little heat and warmth that only planets in very close orbits around them would not be frozen solid, and in such close orbits, these planets would be tidally locked to the star, whereas the long lifetimes of red dwarfs could allow the development of habitable environments on planets with thick atmospheres.
Methods
Studying terrestrial extremophiles
Astrobiological research concerning the study of habitable environments in the Solar System and beyond utilises methods within the geosciences.
